video.title: Why Did David Pour Out the WATER His Mighty Men Risked Their Lives For? (2 Samuel 23)
video.description:
David pouring out the water from the well of Bethlehem, the water his three mighty men risked their lives to bring him, is one of the strangest moments in the Old Testament. Why would a thirsty king empty the very thing he longed for onto the ground, and then call it blood?

In this study we walk slowly through 2 Samuel 23:13 to 17 and its parallel in 1 Chronicles 11, beginning in the cave of Adullam, where a band of men in distress, in debt and discontented first gathered around a fugitive David. We look at the Hebrew word for his longing, the same root behind Israel's craving for meat in Numbers 11 and the place called the graves of craving, and we notice how both cries open with the same little word, who. We follow the three men as they break through the Philistine host, and we hear David answer with the same word he once spoke in another cave, when Saul's life was within his reach. Then we open the Law of Moses: why life is in the blood, why Israel was told to pour blood on the earth as water, and why David seems to do the reverse by pouring water on the earth as though it were blood. We trace the long biblical practice of poured out offerings, from Jacob's pillar of stone to Samuel at Mizpeh and the water pouring at the Feast of Tabernacles. We consider how the scene can be read alongside another Son of David from Bethlehem who offers his cup instead of refusing it, and the apostle who, by strong early tradition, spoke of his own life being poured out. Finally we face the hard shadow of the story in Uriah the Hittite, one of David's own mighty men, and ask what it means for us to receive gifts that others paid for.

Which part of this story spoke to you most? Share your thoughts in the comments, even a single sentence helps others find this study. If you want to keep reading Scripture slowly and carefully together, subscribe to the channel.

Sources mentioned:
King James Version (KJV)
New International Version (NIV)
Mishnah, tractate Sukkah

transcript.text: It is harvest time in Judah, and David is hiding.
A Philistine army is camped in the valley below him.
Their soldiers hold his hometown.
Three of his men come back through enemy lines, carrying water from a well by the gate of Bethlehem.
David takes it, then he pours it out on the ground.
You know this story.
But here is the question almost nobody stops to ask:
Why would a thirsty man pour out the very water he longed for and then call it blood?
It looks like waste.
It almost looks ungrateful.
Three men have just gambled their lives, and their commander empties the prize in front of them.
But David is not throwing it away.
Listen to how 2 Samuel 23:16 puts it:
"Nevertheless, he would not drink thereof, but poured it out unto the Lord."
"Unto the Lord."
The Hebrew verb behind "poured it out" is nasakh.
It is not the word for spilling something.
It is the word Israel used for pouring out a drink offering before God.
David is not emptying a vessel.
He is making an offering.
And watch where it goes.
Not onto an altar, onto the ground.
Notice the town, too.
Of all the water in Judah, David asked for the water of Bethlehem.
Keep that town in mind; it will come back.
But this is where the scene gets stranger.
In the tabernacle, a drink offering was normally wine, poured out with the sacrifice at the altar.
David has no altar here.
He has no priest.
He has no wine.
He has a little water and a group of exhausted men watching him.
So, what does David see in that water that the three men who carried it do not?
Let us look at where he is standing.
Verse 13 says:
"And three of the thirty chief went down, and came to David in the harvest time unto the cave of Adullam.
And the troop of the Philistines pitched in the valley of Rephaim."
Verse 14:
"And David was then in an hold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then in Bethlehem."
The cave of Adullam is not a random place in David's story.
It is where his life as a fugitive began.
First Samuel 22:1 says that when David ran from Saul, he escaped to the cave Adullam.
And then something unexpected happened.
Verse 2:
"And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him;
and he became a captain over them.
And there were with him about four hundred men."
Sit with that.
These were not polished soldiers.
They were men in trouble, men who owed money, men with bitter souls.
That is how the mighty men of David began.
A cave full of people nobody else wanted.
The word for that hold, the stronghold where David waits, is metsudah.
It means a fortress, a high place that is hard to reach.
David lived in places like this for years.
And just one chapter before our story, in Second Samuel 22, David sings a song that uses the very same word for God.
Verse 2:
"The Lord is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer."
My fortress.
My metsudah.
The man hiding in a stronghold already knew who his real stronghold was.
When did this happen?
The text does not give us a date, but Second Samuel chapter 5 tells of a moment right after David was anointed king over all Israel.
Verse 17 says that when the Philistines heard of it, David went down to the hold.

transcript.text: And he called the name of that place Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people that lusted.
Kibroth-hattaavah, the graves of craving.
Israel's craving was satisfied, and it became a graveyard.
David's craving is about to be satisfied too.
The question is what he will do with it.
Look at what David does not do in verse 15.
He gives no order.
He does not say, go and get it.
He simply speaks a longing out loud, the way a homesick man does.
Bethlehem was home.
First Samuel 17:15 says that David went and returned from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem.
Those were his fields.
That was his gate.
Now, a Philistine garrison held his town, and three men heard him.
Verse 16,
And the three mighty men brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David.
The text does not tell us who these three were.
Verse 13 only calls them three of the thirty chief.
Some readers identify them with the three champions named just before in verses 8 to 12.
Others think they are three different men.
The text leaves it open, and so should we.
But look at the verbs,
break through, drew, took, brought.
Four verbs back-to-back, and not a wasted word.
The Philistines held the town itself.
These men went into the enemy's camp, drew water from a well in a town the enemy held, and carried the water all the way back to a stronghold in the hills.
And the narrator closes the story with a single line in verse 17,
These things did these three mighty men.
Notice what that sentence includes.
It does not stop at the raid.
It sets the raid and the pouring out side by side, and lets them stand together as what these men did.
Their water was never drunk, and the text still remembers it.
Then comes the line readers have puzzled over for centuries.
Nevertheless, he would not drink thereof, but poured it out unto the Lord.
And he said, be it far from me, O Lord, that I should do this.
Be it far from me is one Hebrew word, chalilah.
Most lexicons connect it to a root that means to profane, to make something common.
So the sense is close to this.
That would be a profane thing.
It would be desecration.
And David has said this word before in another cave.
In 1 Samuel chapter 24, Saul is hunting David.
He walks into a cave near En Gedi, not knowing that David and his men are sitting in the sides of that very cave.
David's men whisper that God has delivered his enemy into his hand.
David creeps close and cuts off the skirt of Saul's robe.
Then his heart strikes him.
Verse 6,
And he said unto his men, the Lord forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the Lord's anointed.
The Lord forbid is chalilah again.
And in Hebrew, the phrase is almost identical to the one in 2 Samuel 23.

transcript.text: David had water and he poured it on the earth like blood.
The verb in Deuteronomy is a different one, shafhakh, the ordinary word for pouring out.
So we should not claim David is quoting that verse, but the logic underneath is the same.
Life is not yours to consume.
When you hold life in your hands, you give it back to God on the ground.
David looked at that water and in his eyes it had become nephesh.
It had become the life of his men.
And a man of Israel does not drink life, he pours it out.
And David knew what it was to thirst with his whole nephesh.
Psalm 63 carries a heading that places it when he was in the wilderness of Judah.
Verse 1, O God, thou art my God, early will I seek thee.
My soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land where no water is.
My soul thirsteth, my nephesh is thirsty.
The man who wrote that line knew the difference between the water a body needs and the thirst only God can answer.
That is what the three men did not see when they handed it to him.
They saw a gift of water, David saw their blood.
Now the first Hebrew word comes back.
Remember, nasakh, the verb of the drink offering.
The offering itself is called a nesek, and it was poured out beside the sacrifice.
Numbers chapter 28 verse 7 says of the daily offering, in the holy place shalt thou cause the strong wine to be poured unto the Lord for a drink offering.
Every morning and every evening wine went out before God, not drunk, poured.
And long before there was a tabernacle, a man did this in the open.
Genesis 35:14.
And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he talked with him, even a pillar of stone, and he poured a drink offering thereon, and he poured oil thereon.
Not on an altar, but on a pillar of stone.
No priest, just a man pouring something out in the place where God had met him.
There is even a moment in Israel's story when what was poured out was water.
First Samuel 7:6.
Israel gathered at Mizpah and drew water and poured it out before the Lord, and fasted on that day and said there, we have sinned against the Lord.
Water poured before God as an act of surrender.
Much later, Jewish worship kept a water pouring alive at the Feast of Tabernacles.
The Mishnah in tractate Sukkah describes a priest filling a golden flask at the pool of Siloam and pouring that water out at the altar.
So David is not inventing something strange in that cave.
He is standing inside a long tradition.
When something is too precious to keep, you give it to God.
And now we can go back to the town, Bethlehem.
In Hebrew, Beit Lechem, the house of bread.
David longed for water from the house of bread, and he would not drink it because it had cost the blood of other men.
About 1000 years later, another son of David was born in that same town.
